There is a particular kind of quiet that arrives just before dawn, when the world seems to be holding its breath. The streets are empty, the sky is not yet blue, and even the most ordinary things—the corner shop shutter, a puddle reflecting a streetlamp, a bird deciding whether to sing—feel slightly enchanted. I have always liked that hour because it asks nothing of anyone. It does not demand productivity, cheerfulness, or certainty. It simply exists, patient and unannounced.

It reminds me that much of life is made not of great events, but of small repetitions: making tea, tying shoes, opening windows, answering messages, closing them again. These gestures can seem forgettable, yet they are the scaffolding of a life. A person is often revealed less by what they claim to believe than by how they move through these ordinary rituals—whether they rush through them in frustration or meet them with some measure of attention.

Attention, I think, is a form of love. To notice the grain in a wooden table, the way rain gathers on a leaf, the exact shade of tiredness in a friend’s voice—these are not trivial things. They are the texture of being alive. In a noisy world, paying attention can feel almost rebellious. It says: this moment matters enough to be seen.

And perhaps that is all anyone is ever really trying to do: to see and be seen, briefly and honestly, before the light changes.
